frontHtml: Identify Staphylococcus saprophyticus from its setting and laboratory features (coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant).
backHtml: coagulase-negative staphylococcal cystitis in a young sexually active woman with novobiocin resistance is S. saprophyticus .

frontHtml: Link P fimbriae of uropathogenic E. coli to ascending pyelonephritis.
backHtml: P fimbriae are the E. coli adhesin most linked to ascending pyelonephritis.

frontHtml: Explain how urease-producing organisms such as Proteus cause struvite staghorn calculi.
backHtml: alkaline urine plus a staghorn calculus means a urease-producing organism and struvite.

frontHtml: Use white blood cell casts to localise urinary infection to the kidney.
backHtml: white blood cell casts localise a UTI to the kidney.

frontHtml: Recognise genitourinary tuberculosis as a cause of sterile pyuria and choose mycobacterial urine testing.
backHtml: sterile pyuria plus hematuria and a deformed collecting system points to renal tuberculosis.

frontHtml: Associate Schistosoma haematobium infection with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
backHtml: chronic bladder irritation, classically schistosomiasis, leads to squamous metaplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Recognise xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis from its setting and histology.
backHtml: staghorn stone, chronic infection and foamy macrophages replacing the kidney is xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

frontHtml: Recognise BK polyomavirus nephropathy in a kidney transplant recipient and reduce immunosuppression.
backHtml: BK virus nephropathy in a kidney graft is treated by reducing immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Treat acute uncomplicated cystitis empirically with a first-line agent.
backHtml: treat typical uncomplicated cystitis empirically with a first-line agent; culture is for complicated, recurrent or atypical cases.

frontHtml: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.
backHtml: screen once early in pregnancy and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.

frontHtml: Avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults.
backHtml: outside pregnancy and planned urologic procedures, do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

frontHtml: Manage stable acute pyelonephritis with a urine culture and an oral agent that reaches renal tissue.
backHtml: stable pyelonephritis: culture, then an oral fluoroquinolone (or susceptible trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole); admit only for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy or obstruction.

frontHtml: Decompress an obstructed, infected kidney urgently before definitive stone treatment.
backHtml: stone plus obstruction plus infection means drain first, treat the stone later.

frontHtml: Recognise emphysematous pyelonephritis and arrange source control.
backHtml: emphysematous pyelonephritis needs source control (percutaneous drainage, or nephrectomy) plus antibiotics.

frontHtml: Prevent recurrent UTI in a postmenopausal woman with vaginal estrogen.
backHtml: for recurrent UTI after menopause with atrophy, start vaginal estrogen.

frontHtml: Manage catheter-associated UTI by replacing the catheter and culturing from the new one.
backHtml: in catheter-associated UTI, replace a long-dwelling catheter and culture from the new one before antibiotics.

frontHtml: Admit and treat pyelonephritis in pregnancy with an intravenous beta-lactam.
backHtml: pyelonephritis in pregnancy means admission and IV beta-lactam therapy.

frontHtml: Prevent recurrent pyelonephritis in pregnancy with suppression or culture surveillance.
backHtml: after pyelonephritis in pregnancy, prevent recurrence with suppression or close culture surveillance until delivery.

frontHtml: Recognise IgA nephropathy from synpharyngitic hematuria with normal complement and predict mesangial IgA deposits.
backHtml: hematuria during a mucosal infection with normal C3 means mesangial IgA deposits.

frontHtml: Recognise Alport syndrome as an inherited defect of type IV collagen.
backHtml: hematuria, deafness and eye lesions with a split GBM point to an inherited type IV collagen defect (Alport syndrome).

frontHtml: Use anti-dsDNA titres and complement levels to follow activity of class IV lupus nephritis.
backHtml: in lupus nephritis, anti-dsDNA and complement levels follow disease activity.

frontHtml: Explain how C3 nephritic factor causes C3 glomerulopathy by stabilising the alternative-pathway convertase.
backHtml: C3 nephritic factor stabilises C3bBb, giving persistent alternative-pathway activation, low C3 and C3-dominant GN.

frontHtml: Recognise HIV-associated nephropathy as collapsing FSGS linked to APOL1 risk variants.
backHtml: HIV, Black ancestry, nephrotic-range proteinuria and big echogenic kidneys mean collapsing FSGS.

frontHtml: Explain the hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome and its link to renal vein thrombosis.
backHtml: nephrotic hypercoagulability comes from urinary antithrombin loss plus increased hepatic procoagulant synthesis.

frontHtml: Link chronic inflammation to AA amyloidosis of the kidney.
backHtml: chronic inflammatory disease plus nephrotic syndrome and Congo red-positive deposits means AA amyloidosis.

frontHtml: Explain how ACE inhibitors protect the diabetic kidney through efferent arteriolar dilation.
backHtml: RAS blockade protects the diabetic kidney by lowering intraglomerular pressure through efferent dilation.

frontHtml: Identify drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis as a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
backHtml: drug-induced AIN is mainly a type IV hypersensitivity reaction in the interstitium.

frontHtml: Start immediate induction therapy for ANCA-associated rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
backHtml: ANCA-positive rapidly progressive GN is treated at once with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide; do not wait for the biopsy.

frontHtml: Manage post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis supportively with salt and fluid restriction and a loop diuretic.
backHtml: post-streptococcal GN is managed supportively; immunosuppression and biopsy are not routine.

frontHtml: Start maximal RAS blockade as first-line therapy for IgA nephropathy with proteinuria.
backHtml: first-line treatment for IgA nephropathy with proteinuria is maximal RAS blockade with blood pressure control (plus an SGLT2 inhibitor).

frontHtml: Evaluate for malignancy in PLA2R-negative membranous nephropathy with red flags.
backHtml: PLA2R-negative membranous nephropathy in an older adult should prompt a search for a secondary cause, especially cancer.

frontHtml: Diagnose renal vein thrombosis in nephrotic syndrome with venous imaging.
backHtml: acute flank pain and hematuria in a nephrotic patient means renal vein thrombosis until venous imaging says otherwise.

frontHtml: Biopsy the kidney when a patient with lupus develops proteinuria with an active sediment.
backHtml: in lupus, proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, an active sediment or a rising creatinine is an indication for kidney biopsy.

frontHtml: Choose glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate for induction of class IV lupus nephritis.
backHtml: induct class III or IV lupus nephritis with glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate (or low-dose cyclophosphamide).

frontHtml: Switch mycophenolate to azathioprine and continue hydroxychloroquine before pregnancy in lupus nephritis.
backHtml: before pregnancy in lupus nephritis, switch mycophenolate to azathioprine and keep hydroxychloroquine.

frontHtml: Stop the culprit drug as the first step in proton pump inhibitor-induced interstitial nephritis.
backHtml: suspected drug-induced AIN: stop the culprit drug first.

frontHtml: Recognise subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm as an extrarenal complication of ADPKD.
backHtml: ADPKD plus subarachnoid hemorrhage means a ruptured berry aneurysm.

frontHtml: Explain how vasopressin V2 antagonism slows cyst growth in ADPKD.
backHtml: tolvaptan slows ADPKD by cutting vasopressin-driven cAMP in cyst epithelium.

frontHtml: Associate autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease with congenital hepatic fibrosis and the Potter sequence.
backHtml: ARPKD pairs collecting duct cysts with congenital hepatic fibrosis.

frontHtml: Link renal angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex to loss of TSC1/TSC2 control of mTORC1.
backHtml: tuberous sclerosis = loss of the hamartin-tuberin brake on mTORC1.

frontHtml: Use macroscopic fat on CT to identify a renal angiomyolipoma.
backHtml: fat in a renal mass on CT means angiomyolipoma.

frontHtml: Identify renal oncocytoma and its mitochondria-rich cells.
backHtml: oncocytes are pink because they are full of mitochondria.

frontHtml: Recognise medullary sponge kidney as a cause of recurrent stones with preserved kidney function.
backHtml: normal-sized kidneys, medullary contrast streaks and recurrent stones point to medullary sponge kidney.

frontHtml: Associate acquired cystic kidney disease on dialysis with renal cell carcinoma.
backHtml: acquired cystic disease of dialysis raises the risk of renal cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Explain renin-angiotensin-driven hypertension early in ADPKD.
backHtml: early ADPKD hypertension is renin driven, from cyst compression of intrarenal vessels.

frontHtml: Manage an incidental Bosniak I simple renal cyst with no follow-up.
backHtml: Bosniak I and II cysts are benign and need no follow-up.

frontHtml: Screen for intracranial aneurysm with MR angiography in ADPKD with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
backHtml: screen ADPKD patients with a family history of aneurysm or SAH using MR angiography.

frontHtml: Choose an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first-line treatment for hypertension in ADPKD.
backHtml: ACE inhibitor or ARB first for hypertension in ADPKD.

frontHtml: Identify rapidly progressive ADPKD and add tolvaptan.
backHtml: add tolvaptan for adults with ADPKD at risk of rapid progression.

frontHtml: Monitor liver tests during tolvaptan therapy.
backHtml: monitor liver tests on tolvaptan.

frontHtml: Treat infected renal cysts in ADPKD with a lipid-soluble, cyst-penetrating antibiotic.
backHtml: treat ADPKD cyst infection with a cyst-penetrating antibiotic such as a fluoroquinolone.

frontHtml: Treat acute hemorrhage from a renal angiomyolipoma with selective arterial embolisation.
backHtml: bleeding angiomyolipoma: resuscitate, then selective arterial embolisation.

frontHtml: Treat a Bosniak IV renal cyst with partial nephrectomy in a fit patient.
backHtml: Bosniak IV (and most III) cysts are treated as cancer; prefer partial nephrectomy for small lesions.

frontHtml: Explain how VHL loss causes clear cell renal cell carcinoma through HIF accumulation.
backHtml: VHL loss stabilises HIF, causing angiogenesis and clear cell RCC.

frontHtml: Recognise PTH-related peptide secretion by renal cell carcinoma as a cause of hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.
backHtml: hypercalcemia with low PTH and a renal mass means PTHrP from renal cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Link a nondecompressing left varicocele to obstruction of the left renal vein by renal cell carcinoma.
backHtml: a new left varicocele that persists supine in an older man means look for a left renal mass.

frontHtml: Identify WAGR syndrome and its 11p13 deletion as a cause of Wilms tumour.
backHtml: WAGR = 11p13 deletion of WT1 and PAX6 .

frontHtml: Recognise Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome as an imprinting disorder at 11p15.5 that predisposes to Wilms tumour.
backHtml: Beckwith-Wiedemann is an 11p15.5 imprinting disorder that predisposes to Wilms tumour.

frontHtml: Identify acrolein as the cyclophosphamide metabolite causing hemorrhagic cystitis and bladder cancer.
backHtml: cyclophosphamide's metabolite acrolein causes hemorrhagic cystitis and bladder cancer; mesna protects.

frontHtml: Associate phenacetin analgesic use with papillary necrosis and urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
backHtml: phenacetin causes papillary necrosis and upper-tract urothelial carcinoma.

frontHtml: Describe intravesical BCG as live attenuated M. bovis immunotherapy for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
backHtml: intravesical BCG is live M. bovis immunotherapy for high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

frontHtml: Link the adverse-effect profile of VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors to their use in renal cell carcinoma.
backHtml: hypertension, proteinuria, hand-foot reaction and hypothyroidism on an oral RCC drug point to a VEGF receptor TKI.

frontHtml: Evaluate gross hematuria in a high-risk patient with CT urography and cystoscopy.
backHtml: gross hematuria, even on anticoagulants, needs CT urography plus cystoscopy.

frontHtml: Treat high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer with intravesical BCG after TURBT.
backHtml: high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer or carcinoma in situ: TURBT then intravesical BCG.

frontHtml: Confirm dipstick hematuria with urine microscopy.
backHtml: confirm a positive dipstick with urine microscopy before working up hematuria.

frontHtml: Treat a small localised renal mass in a fit patient with partial nephrectomy.
backHtml: small localised renal masses in fit patients: partial nephrectomy.

frontHtml: Choose immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination therapy for metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
backHtml: metastatic clear cell RCC is treated first with checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations, not chemotherapy.

frontHtml: Choose abdominal ultrasonography as the initial study for a suspected Wilms tumour.
backHtml: abdominal mass in a young child: ultrasound first.

frontHtml: Arrange abdominal ultrasound and AFP surveillance in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
backHtml: Beckwith-Wiedemann: ultrasound every 3 months until about 7, plus AFP in early childhood.

frontHtml: Treat localised muscle-invasive bladder cancer with neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy and radical cystectomy.
backHtml: muscle-invasive bladder cancer: neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, then radical cystectomy.

frontHtml: Explain why glomerular hematuria produces dysmorphic red cells.
backHtml: dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts place hematuria in the glomerulus.

frontHtml: Distinguish myoglobinuria from hematuria and hemoglobinuria using the dipstick, microscopy and plasma colour.
backHtml: heme-positive urine without red cells plus clear plasma means myoglobinuria; check creatine kinase.

frontHtml: Recognise overflow proteinuria from light chains as a cause of dipstick-negative proteinuria.
backHtml: trace dipstick protein with a high total protein ratio means non-albumin protein, classically light chains.

frontHtml: Explain how sickle cell trait causes hematuria and impaired urine concentration.
backHtml: sickle cell trait can cause painless hematuria and a concentrating defect through medullary sickling.

frontHtml: Recognise tubular proteinuria from proximal tubule injury.
backHtml: low-molecular-weight proteinuria (beta-2 microglobulin) plus normoglycemic glucosuria points to proximal tubule injury.

frontHtml: Identify oval fat bodies with a Maltese cross as a sign of nephrotic syndrome.
backHtml: Maltese-cross lipid bodies in urine mean lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome.

frontHtml: Link urine that darkens on standing to alkaptonuria and its enzyme defect.
backHtml: urine that blackens on standing plus dark cartilage and early arthritis is alkaptonuria.

frontHtml: Match muddy brown granular casts to acute tubular necrosis.
backHtml: muddy brown granular casts mean acute tubular necrosis.

frontHtml: Use urine osmolality to separate a solute diuresis from a water diuresis.
backHtml: polyuria with urine osmolality at or above plasma is a solute diuresis; with very dilute urine it is a water diuresis.

frontHtml: Evaluate high-risk microscopic hematuria with cystoscopy and CT urography.
backHtml: high-risk microscopic hematuria (older, heavy smoker, many red cells) needs cystoscopy and CT urography.

frontHtml: Confirm dipstick-positive blood with microscopy before evaluating hematuria.
backHtml: confirm a heme-positive dipstick with urine microscopy before any hematuria work-up.

frontHtml: Exclude and relieve bladder outlet obstruction first in acute oliguria.
backHtml: in sudden oliguria, check the bladder first.

frontHtml: Identify hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis using a chart of hemolysis markers and urine findings.
backHtml: heme-positive urine without red cells plus pink plasma and low haptoglobin is hemoglobinuria.

frontHtml: Test for orthostatic proteinuria with a first-morning sample in a healthy adolescent.
backHtml: in a healthy teenager with isolated proteinuria, check a first-morning urine before any work-up.

frontHtml: Reassure a patient with confirmed orthostatic proteinuria.
backHtml: orthostatic proteinuria is benign: reassure and recheck periodically.

frontHtml: Predict the effects of efferent arteriolar constriction on renal plasma flow, GFR and filtration fraction.
backHtml: efferent constriction lowers RPF, raises GFR and raises the filtration fraction.

frontHtml: Calculate creatinine clearance from a timed urine collection.
backHtml: clearance = UV/P; convert urine volume to mL/min first.

frontHtml: Identify hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis as the renal lesion of malignant hypertension.
backHtml: onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis mark malignant hypertension; hyaline arteriolosclerosis marks long-standing benign hypertension and diabetes.

frontHtml: Recognise Liddle syndrome as ENaC gain of function with suppressed renin and aldosterone.
backHtml: hypertension, hypokalemia and suppressed renin and aldosterone that respond to amiloride is Liddle syndrome.

frontHtml: Diagnose type 4 RTA from a hyperkalemic normal anion gap acidosis in diabetic kidney disease.
backHtml: hyperkalemic normal anion gap acidosis with urine pH below 5.5 in diabetes is type 4 RTA.

frontHtml: Localise Fanconi syndrome to the proximal tubule and recognise tenofovir as a cause.
backHtml: glycosuria with normal blood glucose plus phosphate and bicarbonate wasting points to the proximal tubule (Fanconi syndrome).

frontHtml: Identify cystinuria from hexagonal crystals and explain its transporter defect.
backHtml: hexagonal crystals = cystine = defective proximal reabsorption of dibasic amino acids.

frontHtml: Explain enteric hyperoxaluria as the cause of calcium oxalate stones after ileal resection.
backHtml: fat malabsorption causes enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones.

frontHtml: Identify the nephron segments most vulnerable to ischemic acute tubular necrosis.
backHtml: ischemic ATN hits the proximal straight tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb first.

frontHtml: Predict the mineral and hormone pattern of secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD.
backHtml: CKD-MBD: low calcium, high phosphate, low calcitriol, high PTH and high FGF23.

frontHtml: Recognise prerenal AKI from urine indices and treat it with isotonic fluid.
backHtml: FENa below 1%, BUN:creatinine above 20 and bland sediment in a volume-depleted patient: give isotonic fluids.

frontHtml: Treat rhabdomyolysis with early, aggressive isotonic fluids.
backHtml: rhabdomyolysis is treated with early, aggressive isotonic fluids.

frontHtml: Recognise uremic pericarditis as an indication for dialysis.
backHtml: uremic pericarditis is an urgent indication for dialysis.

frontHtml: Add finerenone for persistent albuminuria in type 2 diabetic CKD already on an ACE inhibitor and SGLT2 inhibitor.
backHtml: type 2 diabetes with residual albuminuria on RAS blockade plus SGLT2 inhibitor, eGFR at least 25 and normal potassium: add finerenone.

frontHtml: Correct iron deficiency before starting an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in anemia of CKD.
backHtml: in anemia of CKD, replete iron before starting an ESA, and never target a normal hemoglobin.

frontHtml: Manage an uncomplicated 5–10 mm distal ureteral stone with medical expulsive therapy.
backHtml: uncomplicated distal ureteral stone 5–10 mm: medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin.

frontHtml: Prevent recurrent calcium oxalate stones from hypercalciuria with sodium restriction, normal calcium and a thiazide.
backHtml: recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria: fluids, low sodium, normal calcium and a thiazide.

frontHtml: Prevent tumor lysis syndrome in a high-risk patient with IV fluids and rasburicase.
backHtml: high-risk tumor lysis: IV fluids plus rasburicase (if G6PD is normal).

frontHtml: Start dialysis for established tumor lysis syndrome with oliguric AKI and refractory electrolyte disorders.
backHtml: tumor lysis with oliguria, refractory hyperkalemia, severe hyperphosphatemia or overload needs dialysis.

frontHtml: Predict renin and aldosterone findings in unilateral renal artery stenosis.
backHtml: unilateral renal artery stenosis gives high renin, high aldosterone, and lateralised renin from the stenotic side.

frontHtml: Recognise fibromuscular dysplasia and its usual histologic type.
backHtml: young woman, mid-distal renal artery beading: fibromuscular dysplasia with medial fibroplasia.

frontHtml: Explain the creatinine rise after ACE inhibition in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
backHtml: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR by dilating the efferent arteriole; a large creatinine rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis.

frontHtml: Identify hyaline arteriolosclerosis as the lesion of benign nephrosclerosis.
backHtml: benign nephrosclerosis equals hyaline arteriolosclerosis and small granular kidneys.

frontHtml: Recognise the gross and microscopic kidney changes of malignant hypertension.
backHtml: malignant hypertension: onion-skin arterioles, fibrinoid necrosis and a flea-bitten kidney surface.

frontHtml: Explain the hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome and renal vein thrombosis.
backHtml: nephrotic syndrome (especially membranous) promotes renal vein thrombosis partly by urinary antithrombin loss; a left renal vein clot can cause a left varicocele.

frontHtml: Recognise atheroembolic kidney disease and its biopsy finding.
backHtml: after catheterisation, livedo plus eosinophilia plus slowly rising creatinine means cholesterol emboli with needle-shaped clefts.

frontHtml: Treat scleroderma renal crisis with an ACE inhibitor because it is renin driven.
backHtml: scleroderma renal crisis is renin driven; treat with an ACE inhibitor.

frontHtml: Describe the pattern and type of necrosis in an embolic renal infarct.
backHtml: embolic renal infarcts are pale, wedge-shaped areas of coagulative necrosis.

frontHtml: Identify the receptor that mediates sympathetic renin release.
backHtml: beta-1 stimulation of juxtaglomerular cells releases renin; beta-blockers suppress it.

frontHtml: Manage incidental atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis with optimal medical therapy.
backHtml: most atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is treated medically; revascularise only for specific triggers.

frontHtml: Treat hypertension from renal fibromuscular dysplasia with angioplasty without a stent.
backHtml: renovascular hypertension from fibromuscular dysplasia is treated with balloon angioplasty without stenting.

frontHtml: Treat scleroderma renal crisis with a titrated ACE inhibitor.
backHtml: scleroderma renal crisis is treated with a rapidly titrated ACE inhibitor, continued even on dialysis.

frontHtml: Manage atheroembolic kidney disease supportively.
backHtml: atheroembolic kidney disease is treated supportively; avoid anticoagulation and further procedures when possible.

frontHtml: Confirm suspected renal infarction with contrast-enhanced CT.
backHtml: suspect renal infarction when flank pain with hematuria and high LDH has no stone; confirm with contrast CT.

frontHtml: Treat embolic renal infarction with anticoagulation.
backHtml: embolic renal infarction is treated with anticoagulation and secondary prevention of emboli.

frontHtml: Localise urethral injury after pelvic fracture to the membranous urethra.
backHtml: pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate means posterior (membranous) urethral injury.

frontHtml: Explain the fascial limits of urine extravasation after bulbar urethral injury.
backHtml: extravasation from a bulbar urethral tear spreads to the scrotum, penis and abdominal wall but not the thighs, because Colles and Scarpa fascia attach to the fascia lata.

frontHtml: Explain the pseudo-renal failure of intraperitoneal bladder rupture.
backHtml: intraperitoneal bladder rupture can raise serum urea nitrogen and creatinine by peritoneal reabsorption of urine.

frontHtml: Predict detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia after suprasacral spinal cord injury.
backHtml: suprasacral spinal cord injury gives detrusor overactivity with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, which threatens the upper tracts.

frontHtml: Explain overflow incontinence from diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
backHtml: diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes an underactive detrusor with retention and overflow incontinence.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of beta-3 agonists for overactive bladder.
backHtml: beta-3 agonists (mirabegron, vibegron) relax the detrusor through G s and cAMP and treat overactive bladder without anticholinergic effects.

frontHtml: Recognise posterior urethral valves from prenatal and neonatal findings.
backHtml: a boy with a distended bladder, dilated posterior urethra, bilateral hydronephrosis and oligohydramnios has posterior urethral valves.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanisms of post-obstructive diuresis.
backHtml: post-obstructive diuresis reflects solute (urea) excretion plus a temporary concentrating defect; monitor volume and electrolytes.

frontHtml: Link pudendal nerve injury in childbirth to stress urinary incontinence.
backHtml: the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) supplies the external urethral sphincter; its injury in childbirth contributes to stress incontinence.

frontHtml: Order a retrograde urethrogram before catheterisation when urethral injury is suspected.
backHtml: suspected urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram before a Foley catheter.

frontHtml: Manage complete posterior urethral disruption with suprapubic cystostomy.
backHtml: complete urethral disruption: drain with a suprapubic catheter and repair the urethra later.

frontHtml: Treat intraperitoneal bladder rupture surgically.
backHtml: intraperitoneal bladder rupture needs surgical repair; most extraperitoneal ruptures heal with catheter drainage.

frontHtml: Manage a stable high-grade renal laceration nonoperatively.
backHtml: stable renal trauma, even high grade, is managed nonoperatively; embolise active bleeding and operate for instability.

frontHtml: Choose a beta-3 agonist for overactive bladder in an older adult with cognitive impairment.
backHtml: for overactive bladder in an older adult with cognitive concerns, choose a beta-3 agonist over an antimuscarinic.

frontHtml: Start pelvic floor muscle training for stress urinary incontinence.
backHtml: first-line treatment for stress incontinence is pelvic floor muscle training (plus weight loss); surgery comes after conservative treatment.

frontHtml: Use clean intermittent catheterisation for an areflexic neurogenic bladder.
backHtml: for an underactive neurogenic bladder with a large residual, use clean intermittent catheterisation.

frontHtml: Order voiding cystourethrography when ultrasound is abnormal after a first febrile UTI in a young child.
backHtml: abnormal ultrasound after a first febrile UTI in a toddler calls for voiding cystourethrography.

frontHtml: Explain the low position of a horseshoe kidney and its association with Turner syndrome.
backHtml: horseshoe kidneys are trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery; think Turner syndrome.

frontHtml: Identify pulmonary hypoplasia as the lethal consequence of bilateral renal agenesis.
backHtml: oligohydramnios from absent fetal urine causes Potter sequence; death is from pulmonary hypoplasia.

frontHtml: Distinguish ureteric bud from metanephric mesenchyme derivatives.
backHtml: ureteric bud gives the collecting system (collecting ducts to ureter); metanephric mesenchyme gives the nephron up to the distal tubule.

frontHtml: Name the GDNF–RET signal that induces ureteric bud outgrowth.
backHtml: GDNF from the metanephric mesenchyme acting on RET in the ureteric bud starts kidney development.

frontHtml: Localise congenital obstruction to the ureteropelvic junction.
backHtml: hydronephrosis with a normal-calibre ureter means ureteropelvic junction obstruction; pain after fluid loads is typical in older children.

frontHtml: Apply the Weigert-Meyer pattern to explain continuous incontinence in a girl with a duplex system.
backHtml: a girl with continuous wetness despite normal voiding has an ectopic upper-pole ureter opening below the sphincter.

frontHtml: Recognise the histology and course of multicystic dysplastic kidney.
backHtml: dysplasia shows primitive ducts and cartilage; unilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney leaves amniotic fluid normal.

frontHtml: Identify a patent urachus as a persistent allantoic remnant.
backHtml: urine draining from the umbilicus means a patent urachus, a remnant of the allantois.

frontHtml: Explain the embryologic basis of bladder exstrophy.
backHtml: bladder exstrophy is a failure of infraumbilical mesoderm to reinforce the cloacal membrane, with epispadias and pubic diastasis.

frontHtml: Time the postnatal ultrasound after mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis.
backHtml: for mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis, scan after 48 hours of life; scan early only for bilateral disease or suspected valves.

frontHtml: Counsel about the lethal prognosis of bilateral renal agenesis found prenatally.
backHtml: bilateral renal agenesis is lethal; counsel about prognosis and options rather than offering interventions that cannot change it.

frontHtml: Manage an uncomplicated multicystic dysplastic kidney with serial ultrasonography.
backHtml: multicystic dysplastic kidney is managed with serial ultrasound; surgery is for complications only.

frontHtml: Investigate continuous incontinence in a girl with renal and bladder ultrasonography.
backHtml: a girl who is always damp but voids normally needs renal and bladder ultrasonography to look for a duplex kidney with an ectopic ureter.

frontHtml: Screen for renal anomalies in Turner syndrome with ultrasonography.
backHtml: screen every girl with Turner syndrome with renal ultrasonography at diagnosis.

frontHtml: Evaluate a suspected patent urachus with ultrasonography.
backHtml: suspected patent urachus: ultrasonography first, then surgical excision of the remnant.

frontHtml: Assess suspected ureteropelvic junction obstruction with diuretic renography.
backHtml: for suspected ureteropelvic junction obstruction, diuretic renography shows drainage and split function.

frontHtml: Choose pyeloplasty for symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction with reduced split function.
backHtml: symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction with reduced split function needs pyeloplasty.

frontHtml: Explain how ACE inhibitors reduce GFR by removing angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction.
backHtml: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR by dilating the efferent arteriole; a large creatinine rise suggests renal artery stenosis.

frontHtml: Explain NSAID-induced acute kidney injury through loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation.
backHtml: NSAIDs cause hemodynamic AKI in prostaglandin-dependent states such as heart failure, cirrhosis and volume depletion.

frontHtml: Describe the proximal tubular uptake mechanism of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity.
backHtml: aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity is proximal tubule necrosis from megalin-mediated uptake; it is usually nonoliguric and delayed.

frontHtml: Recognise amphotericin B-induced distal renal tubular acidosis from laboratory values.
backHtml: amphotericin B causes distal RTA with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia by making collecting duct membranes leaky.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
backHtml: lithium causes nephrogenic DI by reducing aquaporin-2 in principal cells; it enters them through ENaC.

frontHtml: Localise tenofovir-induced Fanconi syndrome to the proximal tubule.
backHtml: tenofovir disoproxil causes proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome); tenofovir alafenamide is much less toxic to the kidney.

frontHtml: Recognise acyclovir crystal nephropathy and its mechanism.
backHtml: IV acyclovir, methotrexate, sulfonamides and indinavir cause crystal nephropathy; hydration prevents it.

frontHtml: Explain how mesna prevents cyclophosphamide-induced hemorrhagic cystitis.
backHtml: mesna (with hydration) prevents acrolein-induced hemorrhagic cystitis from cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.

frontHtml: Link nephrogenic systemic fibrosis to gadolinium exposure in advanced kidney disease.
backHtml: gadolinium in advanced CKD or dialysis can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

frontHtml: Recognise the histology of PPI-induced acute interstitial nephritis.
backHtml: PPIs, beta-lactams and NSAIDs cause AIN: sterile pyuria, white cell casts, and an eosinophil-rich interstitial infiltrate.

frontHtml: Use isotonic IV fluids and stop nephrotoxins to reduce contrast-associated AKI in a high-risk patient.
backHtml: prevent contrast-associated AKI with isotonic IV fluids and by stopping nephrotoxins; N-acetylcysteine and prophylactic dialysis do not help.

frontHtml: Continue an ACE inhibitor when creatinine rises by less than about 30% after starting it.
backHtml: after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, accept a creatinine rise of up to about 30% and keep the drug.

frontHtml: Distinguish trimethoprim's inhibition of creatinine secretion from true acute kidney injury.
backHtml: trimethoprim (and cimetidine) can raise creatinine by blocking its secretion; check BUN, urine and cystatin C before calling it AKI.

frontHtml: Manage immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated interstitial nephritis by holding the drug and giving corticosteroids.
backHtml: checkpoint inhibitor AIN: hold the drug and give prednisone.

frontHtml: Replace magnesium to correct refractory hypokalemia in cisplatin-induced magnesium wasting.
backHtml: refractory hypokalemia (often with hypocalcemia) on cisplatin, aminoglycosides or amphotericin: replace magnesium.

frontHtml: Decompress the bladder first in drug-induced acute urinary retention.
backHtml: drug-induced acute urinary retention: catheterise first, then stop the drug and add an alpha blocker.

frontHtml: Diagnose lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from a water deprivation test.
backHtml: no concentration after desmopressin means nephrogenic DI; lithium is the commonest drug cause.

frontHtml: Treat lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with amiloride.
backHtml: amiloride treats lithium-induced nephrogenic DI when lithium must continue.

frontHtml: Identify insulitis as the islet lesion of type 1 diabetes.
backHtml: insulitis with beta-cell loss is the lesion of type 1 diabetes; islet amyloid belongs to type 2.

frontHtml: Recognise glucokinase MODY from its mild, stable, familial phenotype.
backHtml: glucokinase variants reset the beta-cell glucose set point and cause mild, stable, familial fasting hyperglycemia.

frontHtml: Explain how sulfonylureas close beta-cell K-ATP channels and cause hypoglycemia.
backHtml: sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels and cause glucose-independent insulin release, so they cause hypoglycemia; metformin alone does not.

frontHtml: Recognise euglycemic DKA as an adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors.
backHtml: an anion gap ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose in someone on an SGLT2 inhibitor is euglycemic DKA.

frontHtml: Link aldose reductase and sorbitol accumulation to diabetic neuropathy and cataracts.
backHtml: aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, which accumulates in lens, nerve and retina in poorly controlled diabetes.

frontHtml: Attribute the lesions of diabetic nephropathy to nonenzymatic glycation.
backHtml: nonenzymatic glycation drives the basement membrane thickening, mesangial nodules and hyaline arteriolosclerosis of diabetic nephropathy.

frontHtml: Explain the absence of significant ketosis in the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
backHtml: in HHS, residual insulin prevents ketosis but not extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality.

frontHtml: Recognise PPAR-gamma agonism and fluid retention with thiazolidinediones.
backHtml: thiazolidinediones are PPAR-gamma agonists that cause fluid retention, weight gain and heart failure exacerbation.

frontHtml: Confirm a diagnosis of diabetes by repeating the abnormal test when results are discordant.
backHtml: discordant screening tests: repeat the abnormal one before labelling diabetes.

frontHtml: Arrange a retinal examination at the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.
backHtml: in type 2 diabetes, screen for retinopathy at diagnosis; in type 1, start within 5 years of onset.

frontHtml: Choose a GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes when weight loss is a priority.
backHtml: for type 2 diabetes with obesity, add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or tirzepatide.

frontHtml: Deintensify glucose-lowering therapy and stop glyburide in a frail older adult with hypoglycemia.
backHtml: in frail older adults with hypoglycemia, deintensify and stop sulfonylureas, especially glyburide.

frontHtml: Titrate basal insulin to the fasting glucose.
backHtml: high fasting glucose on basal insulin without hypoglycemia: titrate the basal dose up.

frontHtml: Start isotonic fluid resuscitation first in the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
backHtml: HHS: isotonic fluids first, then insulin, with close electrolyte monitoring.

frontHtml: Replace potassium before starting insulin when it is below 3.5 mEq/L.
backHtml: in DKA and HHS, potassium below 3.5 mEq/L means potassium first, insulin second.

frontHtml: Add dextrose and lower the insulin rate when glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL in HHS.
backHtml: add dextrose when glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL in HHS (about 250 mg/dL in DKA) and keep insulin going at a lower rate.

frontHtml: Treat a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer with offloading and debridement.
backHtml: a noninfected neuropathic plantar ulcer with good perfusion heals with offloading and debridement.

frontHtml: Give sick-day advice for type 1 diabetes: continue basal insulin and monitor ketones.
backHtml: on sick days in type 1 diabetes, continue basal insulin and monitor glucose and ketones closely.

frontHtml: Plan pregnancy in type 1 diabetes: optimise glucose and stop teratogenic drugs before conception.
backHtml: type 1 diabetes and planned pregnancy: optimise A1c first, stop ACE inhibitors and statins, add folic acid, check the eyes.

frontHtml: Diagnose insulinoma from the insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin and drug-screen pattern during fasting hypoglycemia.
backHtml: endogenous insulin (high C-peptide and proinsulin) with a negative drug screen during fasting hypoglycemia means insulinoma.

frontHtml: Explain alcohol-related fasting hypoglycemia through the NADH/NAD+ ratio and gluconeogenesis.
backHtml: alcohol causes fasting hypoglycemia by blocking gluconeogenesis through a high NADH/NAD + ratio once glycogen is depleted.

frontHtml: Recognise glucagonoma as an alpha-cell tumour from its clinical features.
backHtml: necrolytic migratory erythema plus diabetes and thrombosis means an alpha-cell glucagonoma.

frontHtml: Explain the cAMP-mediated secretory diarrhea of VIPoma.
backHtml: VIPoma causes secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydria through cAMP-driven chloride secretion.

frontHtml: Recognise IGF-2-mediated non-islet cell tumour hypoglycemia from its laboratory pattern.
backHtml: low insulin, low C-peptide and low ketones with a large tumour points to IGF-2-mediated hypoglycemia.

frontHtml: Explain neonatal hypoglycemia in the infant of a mother with diabetes.
backHtml: infants of mothers with diabetes become hypoglycemic after birth because their own hyperplastic beta cells keep secreting insulin.

frontHtml: Treat mild symptomatic hypoglycemia with oral glucose and recheck after 15 minutes.
backHtml: conscious hypoglycemia: 15–20 g of glucose, recheck in 15 minutes.

frontHtml: Treat severe hypoglycemia in an unconscious patient outside hospital with glucagon.
backHtml: unconscious hypoglycemia outside hospital: glucagon, recovery position, nothing by mouth.

frontHtml: Use octreotide for recurrent sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.
backHtml: recurrent hypoglycemia from a sulfonylurea: dextrose plus octreotide, and admit.

frontHtml: Manage hypoglycemia unawareness in type 1 diabetes with CGM and relaxed targets.
backHtml: hypoglycemia unawareness: CGM with alerts and relaxed targets for weeks.

frontHtml: Treat post-bariatric hypoglycemia with dietary changes first.
backHtml: post-meal hypoglycemia after gastric bypass is treated with diet first.

frontHtml: Investigate documented fasting hypoglycemia with a supervised fast and full biochemistry.
backHtml: prove insulin-mediated hypoglycemia biochemically before imaging the pancreas.

frontHtml: Localise a biochemically confirmed insulinoma with cross-sectional imaging first.
backHtml: after biochemical confirmation, localise an insulinoma with pancreatic CT or MRI, then EUS, and remove it.

frontHtml: Screen for insulin secretagogues when insulin and C-peptide are both high.
backHtml: high insulin plus high C-peptide needs a secretagogue screen before pancreatic imaging.

frontHtml: Disclose evidence of factitious hypoglycemia honestly and supportively.
backHtml: disclose a positive secretagogue screen to the patient privately and supportively, and offer psychiatric care.

frontHtml: Recognise a thyroglossal duct cyst and its embryologic origin.
backHtml: a midline neck mass that moves with tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst.

frontHtml: Interpret thyroid tests when thyroxine-binding globulin is raised by estrogen.
backHtml: high total T4 with normal free T4 and TSH means more binding protein, not thyroid disease.

frontHtml: Associate Hashimoto thyroiditis with primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma.
backHtml: rapid thyroid enlargement in long-standing Hashimoto suggests primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of Graves orbitopathy.
backHtml: Graves orbitopathy is autoimmune activation of orbital fibroblasts: glycosaminoglycans plus new fat.

frontHtml: Recognise subacute granulomatous thyroiditis and its histology.
backHtml: painful thyroid, high ESR and low uptake: subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

frontHtml: Link papillary thyroid carcinoma histology to BRAF and RET/PTC alterations.
backHtml: papillary carcinoma nuclei plus psammoma bodies; BRAF V600E or RET/PTC .

frontHtml: Explain why propylthiouracil is preferred in thyroid storm (it blocks peripheral deiodination).
backHtml: PTU blocks both thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

frontHtml: Explain amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism as failure to escape the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.
backHtml: amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism is failure to escape Wolff-Chaikoff, most likely in underlying autoimmune thyroiditis.

frontHtml: Titrate levothyroxine by free T4 in central hypothyroidism.
backHtml: in pituitary disease, dose levothyroxine by free T4, not TSH.

frontHtml: Confirm subclinical hypothyroidism with repeat TSH and free T4 before treatment.
backHtml: confirm subclinical hypothyroidism with repeat testing before treating; treat persistent TSH of 10 or more.

frontHtml: Distinguish factitious thyrotoxicosis from thyroiditis using thyroglobulin when uptake is low.
backHtml: low uptake plus low thyroglobulin points to exogenous thyroid hormone.

frontHtml: Treat myxedema coma with IV levothyroxine plus stress-dose hydrocortisone.
backHtml: myxedema coma: IV hydrocortisone with IV levothyroxine, plus ventilatory and circulatory support.

frontHtml: Recognise and manage suspected thionamide-induced agranulocytosis.
backHtml: fever or sore throat on a thionamide: stop the drug and check the neutrophil count.

frontHtml: Follow a cytologically benign thyroid nodule with ultrasonography.
backHtml: benign FNA in a low- or intermediate-suspicion nodule: ultrasound surveillance.

frontHtml: Recognise nonthyroidal illness syndrome and avoid treating it.
backHtml: in critical illness, low T3 with high reverse T3 needs no treatment; retest after recovery.

frontHtml: Confirm Graves disease with TSH-receptor antibodies.
backHtml: confirm Graves disease with TSH-receptor antibodies (or radioiodine uptake when the picture is unclear).

frontHtml: Avoid radioiodine and choose methimazole or surgery when Graves orbitopathy is moderate to severe and active.
backHtml: with moderate-to-severe active Graves orbitopathy, treat hyperthyroidism with methimazole or surgery, not radioiodine.

frontHtml: Explain pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A as Gs-alpha (GNAS) loss with maternal imprinting.
backHtml: PTH resistance with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy is pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A, a maternally inherited GNAS (Gs-alpha) defect.

frontHtml: Explain the hypocalciuria of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia through CaSR loss of function.
backHtml: Hypercalcemia with normal PTH and a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 in a family is FHH, a CaSR loss-of-function disorder.

frontHtml: Recognise the histology and laboratory pattern of Paget disease of bone.
backHtml: Isolated high alkaline phosphatase with enlarging bones and mosaic lamellar bone is Paget disease.

frontHtml: Explain how hypomagnesemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism.
backHtml: Refractory hypocalcemia with low or normal PTH: check and replace magnesium.

frontHtml: Recognise osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency after bariatric surgery.
backHtml: Low calcium and phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase and PTH, and pseudofractures mean osteomalacia: unmineralised osteoid.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates.
backHtml: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase and kill osteoclasts.

frontHtml: Apply surgical criteria in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism.
backHtml: Primary hyperparathyroidism with calcium >1 mg/dL above normal, osteoporosis, eGFR <60, stones or hypercalciuria, or age <50: refer for parathyroidectomy.

frontHtml: Manage severe hypercalcemia of malignancy with saline, calcitonin and a bisphosphonate.
backHtml: Severe hypercalcemia: saline first, calcitonin for speed, a bisphosphonate (or denosumab) for durability.

frontHtml: Recognise calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia and treat it with glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (lymphoma, granulomas) responds to glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Use calcitriol in chronic hypoparathyroidism.
backHtml: Hypoparathyroidism needs calcium plus active vitamin D (calcitriol); target low-normal calcium.

frontHtml: Screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis with DXA.
backHtml: Screen all women 65 and older for osteoporosis with DXA.

frontHtml: Prevent rebound vertebral fractures when stopping denosumab.
backHtml: Never stop denosumab without starting a bisphosphonate.

frontHtml: Choose intravenous zoledronic acid when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated.
backHtml: Use intravenous zoledronic acid (or denosumab) when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated by esophageal disease.

frontHtml: Correct vitamin D deficiency before giving a potent antiresorptive.
backHtml: Correct vitamin D deficiency and hypocalcemia before zoledronic acid or denosumab.

frontHtml: Explain hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency through increased POMC cleavage.
backHtml: hyperpigmentation in adrenal insufficiency comes from high POMC-derived peptides, so it occurs only in primary disease.

frontHtml: Identify neuroblastoma and its main adverse prognostic marker (MYCN amplification).
backHtml: in neuroblastoma, MYCN amplification predicts aggressive disease.

frontHtml: Explain why beta blockade without prior alpha blockade causes a hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma.
backHtml: in pheochromocytoma, give alpha blockade before any beta blocker.

frontHtml: Recognise licorice-induced apparent mineralocorticoid excess from a low-renin, low-aldosterone pattern.
backHtml: low renin, low aldosterone hypertension with hypokalemia and a history of licorice is apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

frontHtml: Localise ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with nonsuppressible ACTH to an ectopic small cell lung carcinoma.
backHtml: very high, nonsuppressible ACTH with rapid Cushing features and hypokalemia in a smoker suggests ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer.

frontHtml: Treat adrenal crisis with immediate IV hydrocortisone and saline.
backHtml: suspected adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone and saline immediately, never delayed for tests.

frontHtml: Choose morning cortisol, ACTH and cosyntropin stimulation to diagnose primary adrenal insufficiency.
backHtml: suspected adrenal insufficiency in a stable patient: morning cortisol and ACTH, then cosyntropin stimulation.

frontHtml: Replace glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid in primary adrenal insufficiency.
backHtml: primary adrenal insufficiency needs glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid replacement and sick-day education.

frontHtml: Recognise iatrogenic Cushing syndrome from a ritonavir–inhaled fluticasone interaction.
backHtml: cushingoid features with low cortisol and low ACTH mean exogenous glucocorticoid, including inhaled steroid boosted by ritonavir.

frontHtml: Use inferior petrosal sinus sampling for ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with a negative pituitary MRI.
backHtml: ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with a negative or equivocal pituitary MRI: petrosal sinus sampling.

frontHtml: Use adrenal vein sampling to lateralise primary aldosteronism before surgery.
backHtml: in primary aldosteronism, confirm the side with adrenal vein sampling before adrenalectomy in most patients who want surgery.

frontHtml: Prepare a patient with pheochromocytoma for surgery with alpha blockade before beta blockade.
backHtml: prepare for pheochromocytoma surgery with alpha blockade and volume expansion.

frontHtml: Manage a benign-appearing, nonfunctioning adrenal incidentaloma without further follow-up.
backHtml: a small, homogeneous, low-attenuation, nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma needs no follow-up imaging.

frontHtml: Evaluate central precocious puberty in a boy with brain MRI.
backHtml: central precocious puberty in a boy requires brain MRI.

frontHtml: Relate craniopharyngioma to its Rathke pouch origin and typical imaging.
backHtml: craniopharyngioma comes from Rathke pouch remnants and is typically calcified and cystic.

frontHtml: Explain why IGF-1, not GH, is used to monitor GH receptor antagonist therapy.
backHtml: on pegvisomant, monitor IGF-1; GH levels are uninterpretable.

frontHtml: Explain the stalk effect on prolactin through loss of dopamine inhibition.
backHtml: mild hyperprolactinemia with a large nonsecreting mass is the stalk effect.

frontHtml: Link SIADH to V2-receptor-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion.
backHtml: SIADH retains free water through V2-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct.

frontHtml: Recognise failure of lactation as the earliest sign of Sheehan syndrome.
backHtml: postpartum hemorrhage followed by inability to breastfeed suggests Sheehan syndrome.

frontHtml: Start a dopamine agonist for a macroprolactinoma even with visual field loss.
backHtml: prolactinomas, including macroadenomas with field loss, are treated first with a dopamine agonist.

frontHtml: Manage antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia by switching to a prolactin-sparing drug.
backHtml: suspected drug-induced hyperprolactinemia: change the drug safely and recheck before imaging.

frontHtml: Treat pituitary hyperplasia and hyperprolactinemia caused by primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine.
backHtml: check TSH in every patient with hyperprolactinemia; hypothyroidism can mimic a pituitary tumour.

frontHtml: Confirm acromegaly with failure of GH suppression after an oral glucose load.
backHtml: screen acromegaly with IGF-1, confirm with GH non-suppression after oral glucose, then MRI.

frontHtml: Treat persistent acromegaly after surgery with a somatostatin receptor ligand.
backHtml: persistent acromegaly after surgery: start a somatostatin receptor ligand.

frontHtml: Give stress-dose hydrocortisone first in pituitary apoplexy.
backHtml: in pituitary apoplexy, give IV hydrocortisone first.

frontHtml: Replace glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone in central hypothyroidism with ACTH deficiency.
backHtml: in hypopituitarism, replace cortisol before thyroid hormone.

frontHtml: Recognise constitutional delay of growth and puberty and reassure.
backHtml: normal growth velocity with delayed bone age and a family history of late puberty is constitutional delay.

frontHtml: Choose a supervised water deprivation test to evaluate dilute polyuria.
backHtml: confirm and classify diabetes insipidus with a supervised water deprivation test (or stimulated copeptin) before treating.

frontHtml: Interpret a water deprivation test showing central diabetes insipidus.
backHtml: no concentration with dehydration plus a large rise after desmopressin means central DI.

frontHtml: Image the hypothalamus and pituitary after diagnosing central diabetes insipidus.
backHtml: new central DI needs sellar and hypothalamic MRI to find the cause.

frontHtml: Relate ventromedial hypothalamic damage to hyperphagia and obesity.
backHtml: ventromedial hypothalamic damage causes hyperphagia and obesity; lateral damage causes anorexia.

frontHtml: Explain Kallmann syndrome as failed migration of GnRH neurons from the olfactory placode.
backHtml: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia means failed GnRH neuron migration (Kallmann syndrome).

frontHtml: Relate anterior hypothalamic injury to central hyperthermia.
backHtml: anterior hypothalamic damage causes hyperthermia; posterior damage causes poikilothermia.

frontHtml: Trace the leptin-POMC-alpha-MSH-MC4R satiety pathway.
backHtml: leptin → POMC → alpha-MSH → MC4R is the satiety pathway; its defects cause monogenic obesity.

frontHtml: Describe the hormonal pattern of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
backHtml: functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is low GnRH pulsatility with low or normal gonadotropins and low estradiol.

frontHtml: Recognise Langerhans cell histiocytosis as a cause of central diabetes insipidus.
backHtml: lytic bone lesions plus central DI in a child suggests Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

frontHtml: Explain central precocious puberty from a hypothalamic hamartoma.
backHtml: hypothalamic hamartoma causes central precocious puberty through its own GnRH release, often with gelastic seizures.

frontHtml: Treat functional hypothalamic amenorrhea by correcting energy deficit.
backHtml: treat functional hypothalamic amenorrhea by restoring energy balance.

frontHtml: Choose transdermal estradiol with cyclic progestin for bone protection in persistent functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
backHtml: for persistent functional hypothalamic amenorrhea with low bone density, use transdermal estradiol plus cyclic progestin, not the combined pill or bisphosphonates.

frontHtml: Use gonadotropins to induce spermatogenesis in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
backHtml: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with a wish for fertility needs gonadotropins, not testosterone.

frontHtml: Identify opioid-induced suppression of GnRH as a cause of secondary hypogonadism.
backHtml: chronic opioid use is a common reversible cause of secondary hypogonadism.

frontHtml: Recognise neurosarcoidosis as a cause of central diabetes insipidus.
backHtml: central DI plus a thickened stalk and systemic granulomatous disease suggests neurosarcoidosis.

frontHtml: Treat postoperative central diabetes insipidus with desmopressin and monitor for a triphasic response.
backHtml: postoperative central DI: desmopressin with close sodium monitoring, watching for a triphasic course.

frontHtml: Order brain MRI for central precocious puberty in a young girl.
backHtml: central precocious puberty in a young girl or any boy needs brain MRI.

frontHtml: Treat central precocious puberty with a long-acting GnRH agonist.
backHtml: central precocious puberty, including from a hamartoma, is treated with a depot GnRH agonist; surgery is for refractory seizures.

frontHtml: Identify menin as the tumour suppressor lost in MEN1.
backHtml: MEN1 is caused by loss of the menin tumour suppressor, following the two-hit model.

frontHtml: Recognise MEN2B and its association with pheochromocytoma.
backHtml: MEN2B = MTC, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, without hyperparathyroidism.

frontHtml: Trace medullary thyroid carcinoma to neural crest-derived parafollicular C cells.
backHtml: C cells, and therefore medullary thyroid carcinoma, are of neural crest origin, like the adrenal medulla.

frontHtml: Link RET variants to both MEN2A and Hirschsprung disease.
backHtml: RET gain of function causes MEN2; reduced RET function causes Hirschsprung disease, and some MEN2A families have both.

frontHtml: Choose subtotal parathyroidectomy with thymectomy for MEN1 hyperparathyroidism.
backHtml: MEN1 hyperparathyroidism needs subtotal or total parathyroidectomy with thymectomy, not single-gland surgery.

frontHtml: Offer cascade genetic testing to relatives in a family with a known MEN1 variant.
backHtml: offer first-degree relatives targeted testing for a known MEN1 variant; only carriers need surveillance.

frontHtml: Treat a prolactinoma in MEN1 with cabergoline.
backHtml: symptomatic prolactinoma, including in MEN1: cabergoline first.

frontHtml: Offer germline RET testing to every patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma.
backHtml: all patients with MTC get germline RET testing, whatever the family history.

frontHtml: Exclude pheochromocytoma before thyroidectomy in MEN2.
backHtml: in MTC or a RET carrier, check metanephrines before any operation.

frontHtml: Sequence alpha-blockade, adrenalectomy and then thyroidectomy in MEN2.
backHtml: in MEN2 with pheochromocytoma and MTC: alpha-block, remove the pheochromocytoma, then the thyroid.

frontHtml: Time prophylactic thyroidectomy by RET risk class in a child carrier.
backHtml: a child with a high-risk RET variant (codon 634) has prophylactic thyroidectomy by about age 5.

frontHtml: Use calcitonin and CEA to monitor medullary thyroid carcinoma.
backHtml: follow medullary thyroid carcinoma with calcitonin and CEA, not thyroglobulin.

frontHtml: Replace levothyroxine to a normal TSH after thyroidectomy for MTC.
backHtml: after thyroidectomy for MTC, replace thyroid hormone to a normal TSH; do not suppress.

frontHtml: Identify 5α-reductase deficiency from its genital phenotype and high testosterone-to-DHT ratio.
backHtml: 46,XY with female or ambiguous genitalia at birth, virilisation at puberty and a high testosterone-to-DHT ratio is 5α-reductase deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain hypertension in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency by 11-deoxycorticosterone excess.
backHtml: in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, excess 11-deoxycorticosterone causes hypertension and hypokalemia.

frontHtml: Recognise 17α-hydroxylase deficiency from absent puberty, hypertension and hypokalemia.
backHtml: absent puberty plus hypertension and hypokalemia points to 17α-hydroxylase deficiency.

frontHtml: Attribute Müllerian duct regression to AMH from Sertoli cells.
backHtml: AMH from Sertoli cells removes the Müllerian ducts regardless of androgen action.

frontHtml: Explain an ectopic lingual thyroid as failed descent from the foramen cecum.
backHtml: an ectopic lingual thyroid is failed descent from the foramen cecum and a common cause of congenital hypothyroidism.

frontHtml: Treat salt-wasting CAH crisis in a male neonate with saline, dextrose and hydrocortisone.
backHtml: a vomiting 2-week-old with low sodium and high potassium needs saline, dextrose and hydrocortisone for salt-wasting CAH, even with normal genitalia.

frontHtml: Approach a newborn with atypical genitalia with urgent testing and deferred sex assignment.
backHtml: atypical genitalia: explain honestly, evaluate urgently (electrolytes, 17-OHP, karyotype, ultrasound) and assign sex only after the work-up.

frontHtml: Teach sick-day glucocorticoid stress dosing in congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
backHtml: CAH sick-day rules: double or triple oral hydrocortisone for fever; injection and emergency care if vomiting.

frontHtml: Interpret a raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone screen in a preterm infant using adjusted cut-offs.
backHtml: interpret newborn 17-hydroxyprogesterone against gestational age or birth-weight cut-offs; preterm infants often have false-positive results.

frontHtml: Start levothyroxine promptly for congenital hypothyroidism with a markedly raised screening TSH.
backHtml: very high newborn screening TSH: confirm with serum tests and start levothyroxine the same day.

frontHtml: Correct levothyroxine administration in infants before changing the dose.
backHtml: before increasing levothyroxine in an infant, fix how it is given: small volume, away from soy, iron and calcium.

frontHtml: Prioritise cardiac and aortic imaging at diagnosis of Turner syndrome.
backHtml: at a Turner syndrome diagnosis, image the heart and aorta.

frontHtml: Evaluate hypospadias with an undescended testis for a difference of sex development and defer circumcision.
backHtml: hypospadias plus a nonpalpable or undescended testis calls for a DSD evaluation and no circumcision.

frontHtml: Explain testicular atrophy from exogenous androgens via gonadotropin suppression.
backHtml: Anabolic steroids cause testicular atrophy and infertility through suppressed LH and FSH.

frontHtml: Explain amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism by the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.
backHtml: Amiodarone hypothyroidism is failure to escape the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, most often in glands with underlying autoimmune thyroiditis.

frontHtml: Explain lithium-associated hypercalcemia through the calcium-sensing receptor.
backHtml: Lithium causes PTH-dependent hypercalcemia by raising the CaSR set point.

frontHtml: Link antipsychotic D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway to hyperprolactinemia.
backHtml: D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway causes hyperprolactinemia.

frontHtml: Associate anti-CTLA-4 immunotherapy with hypophysitis.
backHtml: Ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) most often causes hypophysitis.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycemic DKA.
backHtml: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose; hold them around surgery and acute illness.

frontHtml: Identify the adrenal enzyme inhibited by etomidate.
backHtml: Etomidate (and metyrapone) inhibit 11-beta-hydroxylase: low cortisol with high 11-deoxycortisol.

frontHtml: Treat adrenal crisis from glucocorticoid withdrawal with immediate IV hydrocortisone.
backHtml: Suspected adrenal crisis: give IV hydrocortisone and fluids immediately; test later.

frontHtml: Plan glucocorticoid tapering and sick-day rules after adrenal crisis.
backHtml: After glucocorticoid-withdrawal adrenal crisis, taper slowly with sick-day rules and an emergency plan.

frontHtml: Differentiate type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis and treat with glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis (destructive, low vascularity) is treated with glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Recognise biotin interference with thyroid immunoassays.
backHtml: Discordant thyroid tests in a patient taking biotin: stop biotin and repeat before further testing.

frontHtml: Manage immune checkpoint inhibitor thyroiditis.
backHtml: PD-1 inhibitor thyroiditis: beta-blocker, continue immunotherapy, monitor for later hypothyroidism.

frontHtml: Treat immune checkpoint inhibitor diabetes with insulin.
backHtml: Checkpoint-inhibitor diabetes is insulin-deficient and permanent: treat with insulin, not steroids.

frontHtml: Treat SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycemic DKA with insulin plus dextrose.
backHtml: Euglycemic DKA: stop the SGLT2 inhibitor; fluids plus insulin infusion with dextrose.

frontHtml: Manage antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia.
backHtml: Antipsychotic hyperprolactinemia: switch to or add aripiprazole if the psychiatric condition permits.

frontHtml: Treat iodine-induced hyperthyroidism after contrast with a beta-blocker and methimazole.
backHtml: Jod-Basedow thyrotoxicosis: beta-blocker plus methimazole; radioiodine is ineffective while iodine-loaded.
